svg.title: Gram-positive vs. gram-negative cell envelopes
svg.desc: Two cross-sections side by side, outside of the cell at the top. Gram-positive: a thick peptidoglycan layer of about 20 to 80 nanometres, threaded by wall teichoic acids (attached to peptidoglycan) and lipoteichoic acids (anchored in the membrane), sitting directly on the plasma membrane; no outer membrane; stains purple because the thick wall traps the crystal violet-iodine complex when alcohol dehydrates it. Gram-negative: from outside in, an outer membrane whose outer leaflet is lipopolysaccharide (O antigen, core, lipid A = endotoxin) with porin channels, Braun's lipoprotein tethering it to a thin peptidoglycan layer of about 2 to 7 nanometres in the periplasmic space, then the plasma membrane; stains pink because alcohol disrupts the outer membrane and the thin wall cannot hold the dye, so safranin colours it.
svg.text: Cross-sections, outside at the top. Layer thickness is schematic.
Teichoic acids (green): wall TA bound to peptidoglycan;
lipoteichoic acid anchored in membrane (TLR2 ligand). No outer
membrane, no LPS. Lysozyme- and penicillin-sensitive.
Outer membrane: outer leaflet of LPS (O antigen – core – lipid
A = endotoxin, TLR4 ligand), porins for small hydrophilic
molecules. Braun's lipoprotein (dashed) ties it to a thin
peptidoglycan layer in the periplasm. Alcohol disrupts the
outer membrane, dye washes out, safranin stains pink.
